questions.q: Orders of 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 30 and 400 dollars have a mean of 61.89 and a median of 20. Why do they differ so much?
options: The median is calculated incorrectly
One extreme value pulls the mean up, while the median only depends on ordering
The mode is 15, which lowers the median
There are nine values, which is an odd count
questions.explain: The mean uses the exact size of every value, so one outlier shifts it a lot; the median is robust to that.

questions.q: Which measure of center works for nominal data such as region?
options: Mean
Median
Mode
Trimmed mean
questions.explain: Only the mode (most frequent category) makes sense for unordered labels.

questions.q: When the mean and median of a numeric column are far apart, what is the most sensible first step?
options: Report the mean and ignore the median
Delete the median from the report
Look at a chart of the distribution, since skew or outliers are likely
Assume the data is normally distributed
questions.explain: A big gap signals skew or outliers, which a plot will reveal.

questions.q: What does stats.trim_mean(s, 0.2) do with nine values?
options: Removes one value from each end (20 percent trimmed from each side, rounded down) and averages the rest
Multiplies the mean by 0.2
Returns the median
Removes 20 percent of the values at random
questions.explain: scipy cuts int(0.2 * 9) = 1 value from each end, then averages the remaining seven.

questions.q: np.average([80, 100], weights=[3, 1]) returns 85.0. What does that show?
options: The first value counts three times as much as the second
The two values are averaged equally
Weights are ignored by numpy
The result is the median
questions.explain: (80*3 + 100*1) / 4 = 85, so the value with weight 3 has triple influence.
